specPoints.text: understand how to classify a substance as an element, compound or mixture
understand that a pure substance has a fixed melting and boiling point, but that a mixture may melt or boil over a range of temperatures

primer.text: You already know from Element, Compound or Mixture how to sort substances into the three classes. This note adds the chemistry sense of the word pure — a single element or a single compound, nothing else — and shows how melting and boiling points give the experimental evidence for it.

lessons.title: What Pure Means in Chemistry
lessons.opening: In everyday talk, pure suggests something natural or untouched. Chemistry means something sharper: a pure substance is one single element or one single compound, with no other substances present. Pure water holds only water molecules; drinking water also carries dissolved ions and added chlorine, so it counts as a mixture even though it looks clean.
keyPoints: Everyday language calls something pure when it seems natural or has nothing added.
In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or a single compound, and nothing else.
Pure water contains only water molecules, with no other substances present.
Drinking water counts as a mixture because it carries dissolved ions and chlorine as well.
A pure substance must classify as an element or a compound, never as a mixture.
Adding anything at all — even another pure substance — produces a mixture.

low.restatement: Pure, in chemistry, means exactly one substance present: one element or one compound. The moment anything else rides along — ions, chlorine, another solid — the sample becomes a mixture. One sample, one substance: that is the whole test, no matter how clean the sample looks.
low.analogy: A solo singer is a single voice; add a second singer and you have a duet — lovely, but no longer one voice.
low.examPointer: If a question says pure, answer in chemistry terms: one substance only, not merely natural or clean.

medium.restatement: The chemical definition is strict: a pure substance is built from a single element or a single compound and nothing beyond it. Drinking water fails the test even though it looks clean, because dissolved ions and chlorine are additional substances mixed in with the water.
medium.analogy: Think of a recipe card that lists flour and nothing else: that is one pure ingredient. Write flour, sugar and eggs on the card and you hold a mixture of three.
medium.examPointer: Questions often dress tap water, mineral water or sea water as pure water — answer that each is water plus dissolved extras, hence a mixture.

check.stem: A carton is labelled pure orange juice. In the chemistry sense, what does that wording actually describe?

options.text: A marketing claim — the juice holds water, sugars and other substances together
options.explanation: Carton juice contains many substances at once, so chemistry classes it as a mixture.

options.text: A true pure substance, because nothing artificial was added
options.explanation: The chemistry test counts how many substances are present, not how natural they are.

options.text: A pure compound, because the label says so
options.explanation: Labels use everyday wording; chemistry counts the substances present instead.

options.text: An element, because it comes from one fruit
options.explanation: One source does not make one substance; the juice still contains many.

check.stem: Drinking water looks clear and tastes of nothing. Why is it still a mixture?

options.text: It contains dissolved ions and chlorine alongside the water molecules
options.explanation: Extras need not be visible; dissolved substances still make the sample a mixture.

options.text: Because water itself is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen
options.explanation: Water is one chemically combined compound, which is exactly what pure can mean.

options.text: Clear liquids are always mixtures
options.explanation: Pure water is a clear liquid too, so clarity decides nothing.

options.text: It becomes a mixture only once chlorine is added at the tap
options.explanation: The dissolved ions are present even before treatment; any extra substance suffices.

check.stem: Which sample is pure by the chemistry definition?

options.text: Distilled water in a sealed bottle
options.explanation: Only water molecules are present, so the sample is one single compound.

options.text: Sea water, because it is entirely natural
options.explanation: Dissolved salt and other substances make sea water a mixture.

options.text: Clean air, because nothing visible floats in it
options.explanation: Air holds nitrogen, oxygen and other gases together — a mixture.

options.text: Table salt dissolved in water, because both parts are pure
options.explanation: Two pure substances mixed still give a mixture.

check.stem: A student says: I added a pinch of pure salt to pure water, so the sample is still pure. What has the student missed?

options.text: Two pure substances together form a mixture; purity allows only one
options.explanation: The definition permits a single element or a single compound, nothing more.

options.text: Salt is not really a pure substance
options.explanation: Salt is a pure compound; the error lies in combining two pure samples.

options.text: Purity depends on the amount added, and a pinch is small
options.explanation: Quantity is irrelevant; any added substance destroys purity.

options.text: The sample stays pure until the salt actually dissolves
options.explanation: Dissolved or not, a second substance makes the sample a mixture.

check.stem: How does a pure substance differ from a mixture in what it can contain?

options.text: A pure substance holds one element or one compound; a mixture holds two or more substances
options.explanation: Count the substances present: one means pure, more than one means mixture.

options.text: Both can hold several elements, as long as they are bonded
options.explanation: Several elements bonded form one compound — that is purity; unbonded elements form a mixture.

options.text: A mixture must contain at least one impure ingredient
options.explanation: Mixtures can be built entirely from pure substances, like salt in pure water.

options.text: A pure substance must be an element
options.explanation: A single compound is just as pure as a single element.

lessons.title: Melting and Boiling Point Evidence
lessons.opening: Purity is not a guess — it shows up in the data. A pure substance melts and boils at one fixed, sharp temperature, while a mixture softens into a range: melting starts lower and boiling creeps higher than the pure values. Melting point analysis turns this into a routine laboratory test for purity, from drug testing to food production.
keyPoints: A pure substance melts and boils at one specific, sharp temperature.
A mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures instead.
Impure samples generally melt lower and boil higher than the pure substance.
Melting and boiling data can therefore distinguish a pure substance from a mixture.
Melting point analysis checks drug purity with an apparatus that heats a tiny sample slowly.
The closer the measured point sits to the data-table value, the purer the sample.

low.restatement: Heat a pure substance and it melts at one sharp temperature; heat a mixture and the melting smears across a range. Impurities push the melting point down and the boiling point up. No reagents are needed — heat, watch, and compare the readings with the data tables.
low.analogy: Pure ice melts at exactly 0 °C in a clean sweep; salty ice starts slumping well below zero and drips out lazily over several degrees.
low.examPointer: Learn both directions: an impurity lowers the melting point and raises the boiling point.

medium.restatement: The experimental test compares measured values against known data: a sharp melting point matching the tables signals one substance present, while a spread signals a mixture. Impurities generally depress the melting point and raise the boiling point relative to the pure substance, and the nearer the reading to the accepted value, the purer the sample.
medium.analogy: A meeting that starts and ends exactly on time suggests one well-run team; one that drifts across an hour suggests several agendas in the room.
medium.examPointer: Describe the technique in full: small sample, slow heating, comparison with data tables.

check.stem: A liquid boils steadily between 101 °C and 103 °C at standard pressure. Pure water boils at 100 °C. What follows?

options.text: The liquid is impure — it boils over a range instead of at one sharp point
options.explanation: A spread of boiling temperatures is the signature of a mixture.

options.text: It is pure water that is slightly warmer than usual
options.explanation: A pure substance has one fixed boiling point; a spread cannot belong to it.

options.text: The thermometer must be faulty, since pure liquids boil over ranges too
options.explanation: Pure liquids boil sharply; the range points to the sample, not the instrument.

options.text: Boiling behaviour says nothing about purity
options.explanation: Range versus fixed point is precisely the evidence the specification asks you to read.

check.stem: Some impurity is mixed into a sample of pure water. What happens to its melting and boiling points?

options.text: The melting point falls, the boiling point rises
options.explanation: Impurities generally lower the melting point and raise the boiling point.

options.text: Both rise
options.explanation: Only the boiling point rises; the melting point moves the other way.

options.text: Both fall
options.explanation: Only the melting point falls; the boiling point moves the other way.

options.text: Both stay fixed but become harder to observe
options.explanation: The values genuinely shift, and they shift in opposite directions.

check.stem: Why does the melting point apparatus heat the sample slowly?

options.text: So that the exact melting point is easier to observe
options.explanation: Slow heating lets the observer catch the precise moment melting begins.

options.text: To melt the sample faster overall
options.explanation: Slow heating is about precision, not speed.

options.text: Because the sample would burn at full power
options.explanation: The concern is resolving the melting moment, not burning.

options.text: To keep the apparatus from overheating
options.explanation: The slow rate serves the reading of the melting point, not the machine.

check.stem: A measured melting point lands close to the data-table value. What does that tell you?

options.text: The sample is relatively pure
options.explanation: Closeness to the accepted value is the marker of high purity.

options.text: The sample must be a mixture
options.explanation: Mixtures read as ranges sitting away from the sharp accepted value.

options.text: The apparatus is well made, whatever the sample
options.explanation: The reading tracks the sample's purity, not the instrument's quality.

options.text: Nothing — only boiling points carry purity information
options.explanation: Melting point data is equally a purity test.

check.stem: A drug laboratory receives a white powder. How does melting point analysis serve its quality check?

options.text: A sharp measured point near the reference marks the batch as pure
options.explanation: Drug purity is routinely assessed this way, with results compared against data tables.

options.text: Melting reveals which drug the powder is, but says nothing about purity
options.explanation: The analysis targets purity; identity comes from matching the value to the reference substance.

options.text: The powder is pure provided it melts at all
options.explanation: Every substance melts; the sharpness and position of the point carry the information.

options.text: Purity needs the boiling point, so solids cannot be tested
options.explanation: Melting point analysis exists precisely because solids need a purity test too.

glossary.definition: A single element or a single compound with no other substances present.
Two or more substances sharing a space without chemical bonds between them.
An electrically charged particle spread through a liquid, too small to see.
The fixed temperature at which a pure substance turns from solid to liquid.
The fixed temperature at which a pure substance turns from liquid to gas.
A laboratory device that heats a tiny sample slowly to reveal its exact melting point.
Any substance mixed into a sample that lowers its purity.

workedExample.prompt: Pure sulfur melts at 114 °C. A student tests a sulfur sample with a melting point apparatus: melting begins at 100 °C and finishes at 113 °C. Is the sample pure or impure? Give your reasoning.
steps: The sample melts over the range 113 - 100 = 13 °C, rather than at a single sharp temperature.
A pure substance has a fixed melting point, so a 13 °C spread means more than one substance is present.
The measured range also sits below the data-book value of 114 °C, as impurities generally lower the melting point.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The sample is impure (a mixture) because it melts over a range of temperatures, 100 °C to 113 °C, instead of at the fixed 114 °C of pure sulfur.
